dx: Acute respiratory distress syndrome after acute gallstone pancreatitis
case: A 47-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital with acute pancreatitis caused by a gallstone in the distal common bile duct. Serum lipase activity is 2,400 U/L (normal 10 to 140). On hospital day 2 she becomes increasingly short of breath. Her temperature is 38.4 °C (101.1 °F), pulse is 118/min, respirations are 34/min, and blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg. Diffuse crackles are heard over both lungs. She is intubated, and arterial PaO2 is 62 mm Hg on an FiO2 of 0.6. A chest x-ray shows bilateral diffuse alveolar opacities. Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is 9 mm Hg (normal 6 to 12), and echocardiography shows normal left ventricular function. The diagnosis is acute respiratory distress syndrome after acute gallstone pancreatitis.

questions.stem: If her lung tissue were examined microscopically on hospital day 4, which of the following findings would most likely be seen?
options: Intra-alveolar hemosiderin-laden macrophages
Hyaline membranes lining alveolar ducts
Polypoid fibroblast plugs in alveolar ducts
Subpleural fibrosis with honeycomb change
approach: Her PaO2/FiO2 ratio is 62/0.6, about 103, with bilateral opacities and a normal wedge pressure, so this is ARDS and not heart failure.
The tissue pattern of ARDS is diffuse alveolar damage.
In the first week (the exudative phase), protein-rich fluid and dead epithelial cells form hyaline membranes along the alveolar ducts and alveoli.
questions.why: Pancreatitis is a classic indirect cause of ARDS. Circulating cytokines and pancreatic enzymes activate neutrophils, which stick in lung capillaries and release proteases and oxygen radicals. Endothelium and type I pneumocytes are injured, so protein-rich fluid leaks into the alveoli. In the exudative phase, during the first week, plasma proteins such as fibrin mix with necrotic epithelial debris and form pink hyaline membranes that line distended alveolar ducts. After about 1 to 2 weeks, the organizing phase begins, with type II pneumocyte proliferation and fibroblast growth. Some survivors are left with interstitial fibrosis.
whyNot: Hemosiderin-laden macrophages (heart failure cells) form when red cells leak into alveoli during chronic pulmonary congestion, as in long-standing left heart failure. Her wedge pressure is normal, and her illness is only days old.
Correct.
Polypoid fibroblast plugs (Masson bodies) are the hallmark of organizing pneumonia. They do not appear on day 4 of acute lung injury.
Subpleural fibrosis with honeycombing is the usual interstitial pneumonia pattern of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, which develops over years.

questions.stem: Her ventilator delivers a tidal volume of 450 mL with a positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) of 10 cm H2O. Peak airway pressure is 40 cm H2O, and the plateau pressure measured during an end-inspiratory pause is 35 cm H2O. Which of the following is closest to the static compliance of her respiratory system, in mL/cm H2O?
approach: Compliance is the change in volume divided by the change in pressure.
Static compliance uses the plateau pressure, measured with no airflow, so it reflects only elastic recoil.
The pressure change is plateau minus PEEP: 35 minus 10 = 25 cm H2O. Compliance = 450/25 = 18 mL/cm H2O, far below the normal of roughly 50 to 100.
questions.why: Compliance tells how easily the lungs and chest wall stretch. A stiff respiratory system needs more pressure for the same volume. In ARDS, edema fluid and loss of surfactant raise alveolar surface tension. By the law of Laplace (pressure = 2 x surface tension / radius), small alveoli then collapse, so each tidal breath goes into fewer open alveoli. The plateau pressure is used because peak pressure also includes the pressure needed to push air through the airways against resistance. Low compliance is why ventilated patients with ARDS are given small tidal volumes and PEEP to keep alveoli open.
whyNot: This value (450/35) forgets to subtract PEEP. Compliance depends on the change in pressure, not the absolute plateau pressure.
This value (450/30) uses the peak pressure. Peak pressure includes airway resistance, so it gives dynamic compliance, not static compliance.
Correct.
This value (450/10) divides by PEEP alone, which is the baseline pressure and not the pressure change that delivered the breath.

topics: Surfactant and the law of Laplace

questions.stem: Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid from her lungs shows reduced surfactant activity. The main lipid of normal surfactant lowers alveolar surface tension very effectively as the alveolar surface shrinks during expiration. Which of the following structural features of this lipid best explains this property?
options: Two saturated palmitate chains that pack tightly
Two polyunsaturated chains that keep the film fluid
A ceramide backbone linked to phosphocholine
A negatively charged inositol head group
approach: The main lipid of surfactant is dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC), a lecithin.
Its two fatty acids are palmitate, a saturated 16-carbon chain with no kinks.
Straight saturated chains pack tightly when the film is compressed, so surface tension can fall to very low values at end expiration.
questions.why: Surfactant is made by type II pneumocytes and stored in lamellar bodies. It is mostly phospholipid, and DPPC is the main one. Because DPPC has two straight saturated chains, a compressed film of it becomes nearly solid and lowers surface tension close to zero, which keeps small alveoli open. Phosphatidylglycerol and surfactant proteins B and C help the film spread and adsorb, while proteins A and D take part in innate defense. Fetal cortisol and thyroid hormone promote surfactant synthesis, and fetal hyperinsulinemia delays it. In ARDS, injured type II cells make less surfactant, and plasma proteins in the alveoli inactivate what remains.
whyNot: Correct.
Unsaturated chains have kinks that stop tight packing. They help the film spread but cannot drive surface tension to very low values.
A ceramide backbone describes sphingomyelin. Sphingomyelin is the reference lipid in the amniotic lecithin to sphingomyelin ratio, not the active surfactant lipid.
Phosphatidylinositol is a minor anionic phospholipid in surfactant. Its charged head group does not explain the very low surface tension that DPPC produces.

questions.stem: To keep her oxygen saturation above 88%, her FiO2 is kept at 0.9 for several days. Breathing high oxygen concentrations increases mitochondrial production of the radical formed when an oxygen molecule accepts a single electron. Which of the following enzymes directly converts this radical to a less reactive product?
options: Catalase
Glutathione reductase
Myeloperoxidase
Superoxide dismutase
approach: Adding one electron to O2 gives superoxide.
Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide and O2.
Catalase and glutathione peroxidase then remove the hydrogen peroxide.
questions.why: With high inspired O2, more O2 is available to pick up single electrons that leak from the mitochondrial electron transport chain, so more superoxide forms. Superoxide dismutase (copper-zinc in the cytosol, manganese in mitochondria) converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide. Catalase and selenium-dependent glutathione peroxidase convert hydrogen peroxide to water. If hydrogen peroxide meets ferrous iron instead, the Fenton reaction forms the hydroxyl radical, which damages membrane lipids, proteins, and DNA. This is why clinicians use the lowest FiO2 that keeps oxygenation adequate. Cigarette smoke adds oxidants to the lung in a similar way.
whyNot: Catalase converts hydrogen peroxide to water and O2. It acts after superoxide dismutase, not on superoxide itself.
Glutathione reductase uses NADPH to regenerate reduced glutathione. It does not act on any oxygen radical directly.
Myeloperoxidase in neutrophils uses hydrogen peroxide and chloride to make hypochlorous acid. It creates oxidants to kill microbes and does not protect the lung.
Correct.

dx: Status asthmaticus with a rising PaCO2 in a child after a viral upper respiratory infection
case: A 9-year-old boy with asthma is brought to the emergency department because of 6 hours of worsening shortness of breath. Three days ago he developed a runny nose and sore throat. He has used his albuterol inhaler every 20 minutes without relief. He sits upright, speaks in single words, and uses his accessory muscles. His temperature is 37.6 °C (99.7 °F), pulse is 136/min, respirations are 36/min, and blood pressure is 104/62 mm Hg. Diffuse wheezes are heard with a prolonged expiratory phase. Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows pH 7.31 (7.35 to 7.45), PaCO2 47 mm Hg (35 to 45), and PaO2 61 mm Hg (75 to 100). The diagnosis is status asthmaticus with a rising PaCO2 after a viral upper respiratory infection.

questions.stem: His systolic blood pressure falls by 18 mm Hg during each inspiration. Which of the following best explains this finding?
options: Large inspiratory swings in pleural pressure
Systemic arteriolar dilation caused by hypoxemia
Dynamic compression of airways during expiration
Vagal withdrawal during each inspiration
approach: A fall in systolic pressure of more than about 10 mm Hg with inspiration is pulsus paradoxus.
In severe asthma he must pull hard against narrowed airways, so pleural pressure becomes very negative during inspiration.
This increases right ventricular filling, pushes the septum toward the left ventricle, and raises left ventricular afterload, so left ventricular output falls with each breath.
questions.why: Pulsus paradoxus is an exaggeration of the normal small fall in systolic pressure during inspiration. In acute asthma it signals a severe attack, because it reflects how hard the patient must work to inhale. Other signs of severe asthma are inability to speak in sentences, accessory muscle use, and a quiet chest. Early in an attack, hyperventilation lowers PaCO2. A PaCO2 that returns to normal or rises, as in this boy, means the respiratory muscles are tiring and respiratory failure is near. Cardiac tamponade is the other classic cause of pulsus paradoxus.
whyNot: Correct.
Hypoxemia does dilate systemic arterioles, but that would lower blood pressure steadily, not with each inspiration.
Dynamic airway compression happens during expiration and causes air trapping. Pulsus paradoxus is a fall in pressure during inspiration.
Vagal withdrawal during inspiration speeds the heart rate (sinus arrhythmia). It does not cause a large inspiratory fall in systolic pressure.

questions.stem: Skin testing last year showed sensitization to house dust mite, and his total serum IgE concentration is increased. During his original sensitization, which of the following cytokines most directly caused his B cells to switch to production of this antibody class?
options: Interferon-gamma
Interleukin-5
Interleukin-12
Interleukin-4
approach: Allergic asthma is a type I hypersensitivity driven by IgE.
Dendritic cells present the allergen to naive CD4 T cells, which become Th2 cells.
Th2 cells make IL-4, which, with CD40 ligand signaling, switches B cells to IgE.
questions.why: Th2 cytokines each have a main job in allergic asthma. IL-4 drives IgE class switching, IL-5 recruits and activates eosinophils, and IL-13 promotes mucus production and airway hyperresponsiveness. IgE binds high-affinity Fc epsilon receptors on mast cells. On re-exposure, allergen cross-links the bound IgE, and mast cells release histamine, leukotrienes C4 and D4, and prostaglandin D2 within minutes (the early phase). Hours later, eosinophils and other recruited cells cause the late phase, with sustained inflammation and obstruction. Viral infections are common triggers of severe attacks in children.
whyNot: Interferon-gamma comes from Th1 cells. It suppresses IgE class switching and favors opsonizing IgG.
IL-5 produces and activates eosinophils and drives the late-phase response. It does not switch B cells to IgE.
IL-12 from macrophages and dendritic cells pushes naive T cells toward Th1 and opposes allergic Th2 responses.
Correct.

questions.stem: In the emergency department, he briefly breathes a mixture of 70% helium and 30% oxygen through a face mask, and his work of breathing decreases. Which of the following best explains this effect?
options: Higher gas viscosity stabilizing laminar airflow
Lower gas density reducing turbulent resistance
Direct relaxation of airway smooth muscle by helium
Greater solubility of oxygen in airway mucus
approach: By Poiseuille law, laminar airflow resistance depends on gas viscosity and varies inversely with the fourth power of the airway radius.
In large and narrowed airways, high velocity makes flow turbulent, and the pressure needed for turbulent flow depends on gas density.
Helium is much less dense than nitrogen, so the mixture lowers the Reynolds number, makes flow more laminar, and reduces the pressure needed to move air.
questions.why: Poiseuille law (R = 8 x viscosity x length / pi x radius to the fourth power) applies to laminar flow. Because radius is raised to the fourth power, bronchoconstriction greatly increases resistance. Where flow is turbulent, density matters more than viscosity. The Reynolds number rises with gas density and velocity, so a low-density gas such as heliox keeps flow more laminar and lowers resistance. Lung volume also matters: at higher volumes, radial traction widens the airways and lowers resistance. Heliox does not treat the inflammation or bronchospasm. It only buys time while bronchodilators and corticosteroids work.
whyNot: Helium's viscosity is slightly higher than that of air. Higher viscosity would raise laminar resistance, not reduce work.
Correct.
Helium is an inert gas with no pharmacologic effect on airway smooth muscle. Bronchodilation comes from beta-2 agonists and anticholinergic drugs.
Helium does not change oxygen solubility, and solubility in mucus does not determine the work of moving gas through the airways.

questions.stem: Thick mucus plugs contribute to airflow obstruction in severe asthma. The main glycoproteins in these plugs carry dense carbohydrate chains attached to serine and threonine residues. In which of the following cellular compartments are these chains added to the proteins?
options: Rough endoplasmic reticulum lumen
Cytosol, on free ribosomes
Golgi apparatus
Lysosomes
approach: Sugars attached to serine or threonine hydroxyl groups are O-linked oligosaccharides.
Mucins are secretory glycoproteins made by goblet cells and submucosal glands.
O-linked glycosylation of secretory proteins takes place in the Golgi apparatus, after the protein leaves the endoplasmic reticulum.
questions.why: Mucins are very large glycoproteins with repeating domains rich in serine, threonine, and proline. Carbohydrate makes up most of their mass. These O-linked chains bind large amounts of water, which gives mucus its gel properties. N-linked glycosylation, on asparagine, starts in the rough endoplasmic reticulum, while the O-linked chains are added in the Golgi. In asthma, IL-13 drives goblet cell hyperplasia, and mucus plugs can block small airways. In chronic bronchitis, submucosal glands enlarge, and in cystic fibrosis, mucus is dehydrated. Each of these impairs clearance.
whyNot: The rough endoplasmic reticulum lumen is where N-linked glycosylation on asparagine begins. The serine and threonine chains of mucins are added later, in the Golgi.
Secretory proteins are made on ribosomes bound to the rough endoplasmic reticulum. Free cytosolic ribosomes make cytosolic proteins, which do not receive mucin-type sugar chains.
Correct.
Lysosomes break down glycoproteins with acid hydrolases. They do not build them.

dx: Centriacinar emphysema with weight loss in a long-term smoker
case: A 64-year-old woman comes to the physician because of shortness of breath that has slowly worsened over 3 years and a 7-kg (15-lb) weight loss over the past year. She has smoked 1.5 packs of cigarettes daily for 45 years. She breathes out through pursed lips. Her BMI is 18.1 kg/m2. The anteroposterior diameter of the chest is increased, and breath sounds are diminished with a prolonged expiratory phase. Spirometry shows an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.52 (normal 0.70 or greater) with little change after a bronchodilator. Serum alpha-1 antitrypsin concentration is normal. Chest CT shows centrilobular emphysema that is most severe in the upper lobes. The diagnosis is centriacinar emphysema.

questions.stem: Her residual volume is 210% of predicted. Which of the following best explains the trapping of air in her lungs during expiration?
options: Hyperplasia of bronchial submucosal glands
Reversible spasm of bronchial smooth muscle
Fibrosis that stiffens alveolar walls
Lost radial traction on small airways
approach: Small airways have no cartilage, so they stay open only because attached alveolar walls pull outward on them.
Emphysema destroys those alveolar walls and the elastic recoil they provide.
During forced or rapid expiration, pleural pressure then squeezes the unsupported airways shut early, trapping air and raising residual volume.
questions.why: Centriacinar emphysema, the type caused by smoking, begins in the respiratory bronchioles and is worst in the upper lobes. Panacinar emphysema, linked to alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, involves the whole acinus and is worst in the lower lobes. In both, loss of alveolar walls removes the tethering that holds small airways open. Airways collapse during expiration, air is trapped, and the chest becomes barrel shaped. Pursed-lip breathing adds back-pressure in the airways, which keeps them open longer and lets more air out.
whyNot: Submucosal gland hyperplasia defines chronic bronchitis. It narrows the large airways with mucus and does not explain collapse of small airways in expiration.
Reversible bronchospasm is typical of asthma. Her obstruction barely changes after a bronchodilator.
Fibrosis increases recoil and pulls airways open. It causes restrictive disease with small lung volumes.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her serum alpha-1 antitrypsin concentration is normal. In a healthy lung, which of the following is the normal protective action of this protein that her smoking has overwhelmed?
options: Cross-linking elastin fibers in the alveolar septa
Irreversibly inhibiting neutrophil elastase
Scavenging oxidants released from cigarette smoke
Blocking neutrophil adhesion to capillary endothelium
approach: Alpha-1 antitrypsin is a serine protease inhibitor (serpin) made in the liver.
It diffuses into the lung and binds neutrophil elastase in a stable complex that inactivates the enzyme.
Smoking tips the balance by recruiting neutrophils and macrophages and by oxidizing the inhibitor, so elastase wins and alveolar walls are destroyed.
questions.why: The lung depends on a balance between proteases and antiproteases. Neutrophil elastase and macrophage metalloproteinases can digest elastin, and alpha-1 antitrypsin is the main defense against elastase. Cigarette smoke draws neutrophils and macrophages into the respiratory bronchioles, where smoke particles deposit, so more protease is released there. Oxidants in smoke also oxidize a methionine at the inhibitor's active site, which lowers its activity. The result is centriacinar emphysema, even when the inhibitor level is normal. With inherited deficiency (PiZZ), the same imbalance occurs at a younger age and favors the lower lobes.
whyNot: Elastin is cross-linked by lysyl oxidase, a copper-dependent enzyme. Alpha-1 antitrypsin does not build elastin.
Correct.
Antioxidants such as glutathione and superoxide dismutase scavenge oxidants. Alpha-1 antitrypsin is itself a target of smoke oxidants.
Neutrophil adhesion depends on selectins and integrins. Alpha-1 antitrypsin acts on the enzyme neutrophils release, not on their adhesion.

questions.stem: Her brother is also a long-term smoker. He has COPD dominated by chronic bronchitis, and his FEV1 is the same as hers. Compared with her brother, she is more likely to have which of the following?
options: Lower DLCO and higher PaO2
Lower DLCO and lower PaO2
Higher DLCO and higher PaO2
Higher DLCO and lower PaO2
approach: DLCO depends on the surface area of the alveolar-capillary membrane. Emphysema destroys alveolar walls and their capillaries, so DLCO falls.
Because ventilation and perfusion are lost together, ventilation-perfusion matching is fairly preserved in emphysema, and PaO2 stays near normal until late.
In chronic bronchitis the alveolar walls are intact (normal DLCO), but mucus-filled airways supply perfused alveoli poorly, causing low ventilation-perfusion ratios and early hypoxemia.
questions.why: Both forms of COPD show an FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.70 with increased total lung capacity and residual volume. The difference lies in the alveoli and the blood gases. Predominant emphysema gives a low DLCO, hyperventilation, and near-normal PaO2 and PaCO2 until late disease. Predominant chronic bronchitis gives a normal DLCO but early hypoxemia and hypercapnia from shunt-like ventilation-perfusion mismatch. Chronic hypoxemia then leads to polycythemia, pulmonary hypertension, and cor pulmonale.
whyNot: Correct.
A low PaO2 early in the disease fits chronic bronchitis better. Emphysema tends to keep PaO2 near normal until late.
A higher DLCO would fit intact alveolar walls, which describes her brother. Her alveolar walls and capillaries are destroyed.
Higher DLCO with lower PaO2 describes chronic bronchitis, which is her brother's pattern, not hers.

questions.stem: Indirect calorimetry shows a resting energy expenditure of 125% of predicted. She has no fever or infection, and her thyroid function is normal. Which of the following features of her lung disease most increases the energy used by her respiratory muscles?
options: Increased elastic recoil of the lungs
Decreased anatomic dead space
Hyperinflation flattening the diaphragm
Lower airway resistance at high lung volumes
approach: Her weight loss with a high resting energy expenditure points to costly breathing.
Hyperinflation flattens and shortens the diaphragm, so it works at a poor point on its length-tension curve.
Her muscles therefore spend more energy and O2 for each breath, on top of the work of overcoming obstruction and air trapping.
questions.why: At rest, breathing normally uses only about 3 to 5 percent of the body's energy. In severe emphysema this rises sharply. A flat diaphragm generates less force per unit of energy, trapped air must be overcome before inspiratory flow begins, and larger dead space means more total ventilation is needed. This higher resting energy expenditure, together with poor intake because eating worsens dyspnea, causes loss of fat and muscle. A low BMI in COPD predicts a worse outcome.
whyNot: Elastic recoil is decreased in emphysema because elastin is destroyed. Increased recoil is a feature of fibrosis.
Anatomic dead space is set by the conducting airways and is not reduced in emphysema. Physiologic dead space actually rises as alveolar capillaries are lost, which adds to the work of breathing.
Correct.
Airway resistance does fall at high lung volumes, but lower resistance would reduce work. Her obstruction comes from airway collapse during expiration.

dx: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax from a ruptured apical bleb in a tall thin young man
case: A 22-year-old man comes to the emergency department 2 hours after the sudden onset of right-sided chest pain and shortness of breath while sitting at his desk. He is 193 cm (6 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 68 kg (150 lb). He smokes cigarettes and has no history of lung disease or trauma. His temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg. Oxygen saturation is 95% on room air. The trachea is midline, and the neck veins are not distended. A chest x-ray shows a thin visceral pleural line separated from the right chest wall, with no lung markings beyond it. CT shows small subpleural blebs at the right lung apex. The diagnosis is primary spontaneous pneumothorax from a ruptured apical bleb.

questions.stem: Which of the following sets of findings is most likely on examination of the right hemithorax?
options: Dull percussion, absent breath sounds, decreased fremitus
Hyperresonance, absent breath sounds, decreased fremitus
Dull percussion, bronchial breath sounds, increased fremitus
Normal resonance, diffuse wheezes, normal fremitus
approach: Air now separates the right lung from the chest wall.
Air in the pleural space makes the percussion note hyperresonant.
The air layer and the collapsed lung block transmission of breath sounds and vocal vibrations, so both are reduced or absent.
questions.why: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs without known lung disease, typically in tall, thin young men, often smokers, when a subpleural apical bleb ruptures. Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax complicates lung disease such as COPD or cystic fibrosis and is more dangerous because lung reserve is already low. Tension pneumothorax occurs when a one-way valve traps air with each breath. Rising pressure shifts the trachea away from the affected side, kinks the great veins, distends the neck veins, and causes hypotension. This man has a midline trachea and normal blood pressure, so his pneumothorax is not under tension.
whyNot: Dullness with absent breath sounds and decreased fremitus describes a pleural effusion, because fluid is dull to percussion.
Correct.
Dullness with bronchial breath sounds and increased fremitus describes lobar consolidation, where solid lung conducts sound well.
Normal resonance with diffuse wheezes describes asthma or another airway disease, not air in the pleural space.

questions.stem: A chest tube is placed in his right fifth intercostal space in the midaxillary line. In a person with normally expanded lungs, if a needle were instead passed through the right ninth intercostal space in the midaxillary line during quiet breathing, which of the following would it most likely enter?
options: Lower lobe of the right lung near its base
Peritoneal cavity beneath the right hemidiaphragm
Middle lobe of the right lung at its lateral edge
Costodiaphragmatic recess of the pleura
approach: In quiet breathing, the inferior border of the lung lies at about rib 6 in the midclavicular line, rib 8 in the midaxillary line, and rib 10 near the vertebrae.
The parietal pleura extends about two ribs lower: rib 8, rib 10, and rib 12 at the same lines.
At the ninth intercostal space in the midaxillary line, the needle lies below the lung but above the lower edge of the pleura, in the costodiaphragmatic recess.
questions.why: The gap between the lower border of the lung and the lower reflection of the pleura forms the costodiaphragmatic recesses. The lungs move into them only on deep inspiration. Pleural fluid collects in these recesses, so thoracentesis is usually done there, while chest tubes for pneumothorax go higher, often in the fourth or fifth intercostal space in the midaxillary line. In both procedures the needle or tube passes just above the upper border of a rib, because the intercostal vein, artery, and nerve run in the costal groove along the lower border of each rib. A needle placed too low can pass through the diaphragm and injure the liver or spleen.
whyNot: The base of the right lower lobe reaches only about rib 8 in the midaxillary line during quiet breathing.
The peritoneal cavity lies below the diaphragm. At this level the pleural recess comes first, though a needle placed too low could reach the liver.
The middle lobe lies anteriorly and does not reach the ninth intercostal space in the midaxillary line.
Correct.

topics: Surface projections of lungs and pleura

questions.stem: When air entered his pleural space, his right lung collapsed toward the hilum. Part of the inward recoil that collapsed the lung comes from a protein in the alveolar walls that stretches and then returns to its resting length. Which of the following correctly pairs this protein with the cofactor required for its cross-linking?
options: Elastin and copper
Type I collagen and vitamin C
Fibrillin and zinc
Type IV collagen and vitamin K
approach: The lung's tendency to recoil comes from surface tension and from elastic fibers in the alveolar walls.
The protein that stretches and recoils is elastin.
Elastin chains are cross-linked through desmosine links formed by lysyl oxidase, an enzyme that requires copper.
questions.why: Elastin is rich in glycine and proline, carries lysine residues that form its cross-links, and is laid down on a fibrillin scaffold. Lysyl oxidase oxidizes lysine side chains so they can join into desmosine cross-links, which let elastin stretch and spring back. Normally the inward recoil of the lung is balanced by the outward recoil of the chest wall, giving a negative intrapleural pressure. When air enters the pleural space, that balance is lost and the lung recoils toward the hilum. Loss of elastin in emphysema increases compliance, while collagen deposition in fibrosis decreases it. Copper deficiency and Menkes disease impair lysyl oxidase.
whyNot: Correct.
Vitamin C is needed to hydroxylate proline and lysine in collagen, while the cross-linking enzyme, lysyl oxidase, needs copper. Type I collagen resists stretch and does not recoil like elastin.
Fibrillin forms the microfibril scaffold for elastin and is defective in Marfan syndrome. It is not cross-linked by a zinc-dependent enzyme.
Type IV collagen forms basement membranes, and vitamin K carboxylates clotting factors. Neither provides elastic recoil.

questions.stem: After his lung re-expands, pulmonary function testing is done. As he inhales from functional residual capacity to total lung capacity, which of the following best describes the change in his pulmonary vascular resistance?
options: Falls, because extra-alveolar vessels are pulled open
Rises, because extra-alveolar vessels lose radial traction
Rises, because alveolar capillaries are compressed
Unchanged, because pulmonary vessels are fully dilated
approach: Pulmonary vascular resistance has a U-shaped relation to lung volume and is lowest at functional residual capacity.
At high lung volumes, expanding alveoli stretch and flatten the capillaries in the alveolar walls.
This rise in alveolar vessel resistance outweighs the widening of extra-alveolar vessels, so total resistance rises.
questions.why: There are two groups of pulmonary vessels. Alveolar vessels are the capillaries in the alveolar walls, and they are compressed as alveoli inflate. Extra-alveolar vessels are the larger arteries and veins in the lung tissue, and they are pulled open by radial traction as the lung expands. At low lung volumes, extra-alveolar vessels narrow, and hypoxic vasoconstriction in poorly ventilated areas adds to resistance. At high lung volumes, compressed alveolar vessels dominate. Resistance is lowest between the two, at functional residual capacity.
whyNot: Extra-alveolar vessels do widen at high volumes, but compression of the alveolar capillaries outweighs this, so total resistance rises.
Extra-alveolar vessels lose radial traction at low lung volumes, not at total lung capacity.
Correct.
Pulmonary vascular resistance changes with lung volume. It is lowest at functional residual capacity, not fixed.

topics: Pulmonary vascular resistance and lung volume

dx: Coal workers pneumoconiosis with progressive massive fibrosis in a retired miner
case: A 71-year-old man who worked as an underground coal miner for 32 years comes to the physician because of shortness of breath that has slowly worsened over 5 years. He sometimes coughs up black sputum. Respirations are 22/min, and oxygen saturation is 91% on room air. Fine crackles are heard over both upper lung fields. Pulmonary function testing shows a total lung capacity of 68% of predicted (normal 80 to 120), an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.82 (normal 0.70 or greater), and a DLCO of 54% of predicted (normal 75 to 125). A chest x-ray shows many small nodules in both upper lobes and large, confluent masses in both upper zones. The diagnosis is coal workers pneumoconiosis with progressive massive fibrosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings is most likely on microscopic examination of his lungs?
options: Lower lobe fibrosis with ferruginous bodies
Noncaseating granulomas with hilar adenopathy
Apical cavities lined by caseating granulomas
Coal-laden macrophages in collagen nodules
approach: Coal dust is inhaled and taken up by alveolar macrophages, which collect around respiratory bronchioles in the upper lobes.
These form coal macules and then nodules of collagen and pigment-laden macrophages.
In progressive massive fibrosis, nodules merge into large black scars, mostly in the upper lobes.
questions.why: Each pneumoconiosis has a typical pattern. Coal workers pneumoconiosis affects the upper lobes with coal macules, nodules, and in some patients progressive massive fibrosis. Silicosis also favors the upper lobes, with hard silicotic nodules, eggshell calcification of hilar nodes, and a higher risk of tuberculosis. Asbestosis affects the lower lobes and shows ferruginous bodies (asbestos fibers coated with iron-containing protein), along with pleural plaques. Berylliosis, seen in aerospace and electronics work, causes noncaseating granulomas from a T cell response to beryllium.
whyNot: Lower lobe fibrosis with ferruginous bodies describes asbestosis.
Noncaseating granulomas with hilar adenopathy suggest berylliosis or sarcoidosis.
Caseating granulomas in apical cavities describe reactivation tuberculosis, a known complication of silicosis.
Correct.

questions.stem: His wife has severe obesity with a BMI of 47 kg/m2, and her total lung capacity is also reduced. Which of the following test results would best distinguish his type of restrictive disease from hers?
options: Diffusing capacity for CO
Ratio of FEV1 to FVC
Total lung capacity by plethysmography
Forced vital capacity
approach: Both have restriction, so both have a reduced total lung capacity, a reduced FVC, and a normal or increased FEV1/FVC ratio.
His restriction is intrinsic: scarring of the lung tissue destroys alveolar-capillary membrane and thickens what remains.
Her restriction is extrapulmonary: her lungs are normal but cannot expand fully, so her DLCO is usually normal while his is reduced.
questions.why: Restrictive disease comes in two kinds. Intrinsic restriction, as in pneumoconiosis or idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, damages the alveolar walls, so DLCO falls and the A-a gradient widens. Extrapulmonary restriction comes from obesity, kyphoscoliosis, or neuromuscular weakness. The lung tissue is healthy, so DLCO is usually normal. Any hypoxemia in extrapulmonary restriction comes mostly from hypoventilation, which raises PaCO2 and keeps the A-a gradient normal.
whyNot: Correct.
The FEV1/FVC ratio is normal or increased in both kinds of restriction, so it cannot separate them.
Total lung capacity is reduced in both. It confirms restriction but does not show where it comes from.
Forced vital capacity falls in both kinds of restriction.

questions.stem: Coal dust that lands on the mucus lining his bronchi is carried up to the pharynx and cleared, but dust that reaches his respiratory bronchioles and alveoli is retained and forms coal macules. Which of the following best explains this difference?
options: Distal cilia beat toward the alveoli instead of the pharynx
Alveolar macrophages destroy ciliated cells in the bronchioles
Distal airspaces lack a mucus blanket moved by cilia
Coal dust paralyzes cilia only in the smallest airways
approach: Mucociliary clearance needs both a mucus layer and beating cilia.
Goblet cells and glands end before the respiratory bronchioles, ciliated cells become sparse there, and alveoli have no cilia.
Dust that reaches these distal airspaces must be engulfed by macrophages, which clear it slowly and collect around respiratory bronchioles.
questions.why: In the conducting airways, inhaled particles stick to a gel layer of mucus that floats on a thin watery periciliary layer. Cilia beat in a coordinated way, moving the mucus toward the pharynx, where it is swallowed or coughed out. Each cilium has a 9 plus 2 axoneme, and dynein arms use ATP to slide the outer microtubule doublets past each other, which bends the cilium. Smoking causes squamous metaplasia and ciliary damage, and ciliary defects such as primary ciliary dyskinesia leave mucus behind and invite infection. Distal particles are left to alveolar macrophages, and in a coal miner these dust-laden macrophages pile up around the respiratory bronchioles.
whyNot: Cilia throughout the airways beat toward the pharynx. Reversed beating would not explain retention.
Alveolar macrophages engulf dust. They do not destroy the ciliated lining of the bronchioles.
Correct.
There is no selective paralysis of distal cilia. The difference reflects the normal structure of the distal airways.

questions.stem: His grandson, a dairy farmer, entered a recently filled corn silo. Several hours later he developed cough, chest tightness, and dyspnea, and a chest x-ray showed pulmonary edema. Six weeks later he again has dyspnea, and CT shows bronchiolitis obliterans. Which of the following inhaled agents most likely caused his illness?
options: Carbon monoxide
Nitrogen dioxide
Hydrogen sulfide
Thermophilic actinomycete spores
approach: Fresh silage ferments and releases nitrogen oxides in the first days to weeks after filling.
Nitrogen dioxide is heavier than air and collects in the silo. It dissolves in airway lining fluid to form nitric acid, injuring bronchioles and alveoli.
The pattern of delayed pulmonary edema followed weeks later by bronchiolitis obliterans is silo-filler disease.
questions.why: Occupational lung diseases are linked to the work and the material. Silo-filler disease follows nitrogen dioxide exposure in a freshly filled silo. Byssinosis comes from cotton dust and causes chest tightness that is worst on the first workday of the week. Bagassosis is hypersensitivity pneumonitis from moldy sugarcane, and farmer lung is hypersensitivity pneumonitis from thermophilic actinomycetes in moldy hay. Because nitrogen dioxide is not very water soluble, it reaches the small airways and alveoli, which explains delayed edema rather than immediate upper airway irritation.
whyNot: Carbon monoxide causes tissue hypoxia by binding hemoglobin. It does not cause pulmonary edema followed by bronchiolitis obliterans.
Correct.
Hydrogen sulfide is found in manure pits and sewers. It mainly causes sudden collapse by inhibiting cytochrome oxidase.
Thermophilic actinomycete spores in moldy hay cause farmer lung, a hypersensitivity pneumonitis with fever and malaise, not edema after silo entry.

dx: Chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis (farmer lung) from moldy hay
case: A 52-year-old woman who runs a dairy farm comes to the physician because of a 2-year history of shortness of breath and dry cough that have slowly worsened. Her symptoms are worse in winter, when she feeds stored hay to her cattle. She has never smoked. Respirations are 20/min, and oxygen saturation is 93% on room air. Inspiratory crackles are heard over both lungs. Pulmonary function testing shows a restrictive pattern with a reduced DLCO. High-resolution CT shows centrilobular ground-glass nodules and fibrosis mainly in the upper and middle lung zones. Transbronchial biopsy shows lymphocytic inflammation centered on bronchioles, poorly formed noncaseating granulomas, and interstitial fibrosis. The diagnosis is chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis (farmer lung) from moldy hay.

questions.stem: Which of the following serologic findings would most strongly support this diagnosis over allergic asthma?
options: Precipitating IgG to actinomycete antigens
Elevated IgE specific to hay dust antigens
Antibodies to cyclic citrullinated peptides
Proteinase 3 antineutrophil antibodies
approach: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is a mix of type III (immune complex) and type IV (T cell) reactions to inhaled organic antigens.
Type III reactions need IgG antibodies against the antigen, which can be shown as serum precipitins.
Allergic asthma is a type I reaction mediated by IgE, so antigen-specific IgE points toward asthma instead.
questions.why: In farmer lung, thermophilic actinomycetes such as Saccharopolyspora rectivirgula and fungi grow in moldy hay. Repeated inhalation produces IgG antibodies. IgG forms immune complexes with the antigen in the alveolar walls and activates complement (type III), and Th1 and CD8 T cells with macrophages form poorly formed granulomas (type IV). Inflammation centers on the bronchioles and alveolar walls. Acute disease brings fever and dyspnea hours after exposure, and chronic disease leads to fibrosis. Asthma, in contrast, causes episodic reversible obstruction with eosinophils and IgE, without fever or granulomas. Precipitins show exposure and are found in some healthy farmers, so they support the diagnosis in the right clinical setting.
whyNot: Correct.
Antigen-specific IgE indicates type I hypersensitivity, as in allergic asthma or rhinitis.
Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies point to rheumatoid arthritis, which can cause interstitial lung disease but not this exposure-linked picture.
Proteinase 3 ANCA points to granulomatosis with polyangiitis, a necrotizing vasculitis of airways and kidneys.

questions.stem: Before her exposure history was recognized, the differential diagnosis included cryptogenic organizing pneumonia. Which of the following biopsy findings would have most strongly supported that diagnosis?
options: Uniform interstitial inflammation and fibrosis
Alveoli packed with pigmented macrophages
Fibroblast plugs filling alveolar ducts
Patchy subpleural fibrosis with honeycombing
approach: Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia is defined by its histology.
Its hallmark is polypoid plugs of loose connective tissue with fibroblasts (Masson bodies) inside bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli.
The other choices are the patterns of other interstitial pneumonias.
questions.why: Several interstitial pneumonias are told apart by their histologic pattern. Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia shows fibroblast plugs in the airspaces, often follows infection or another injury, and usually responds well to corticosteroids. Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia shows uniform interstitial inflammation and fibrosis, all of the same age. Desquamative interstitial pneumonia occurs in smokers, with alveoli filled by pigmented macrophages. Usual interstitial pneumonia, the pattern of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, shows patchy subpleural fibrosis, fibroblastic foci, and honeycombing.
whyNot: Uniform interstitial inflammation and fibrosis of the same age is nonspecific interstitial pneumonia.
Alveoli packed with pigmented macrophages describe desquamative interstitial pneumonia in smokers.
Correct.
Patchy subpleural fibrosis with honeycombing is usual interstitial pneumonia, the pattern of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

questions.stem: Two years ago she was intubated for 3 weeks after a farm accident, and tracheal stenosis was also considered as a cause of her dyspnea. Which of the following flow-volume loop patterns would a fixed tracheal stenosis produce?
options: Scooped expiratory limb with a high total lung capacity
Flattened inspiratory and expiratory limbs
Narrow loop shifted toward low lung volumes
Flattened inspiratory limb with a normal expiratory limb
approach: A fixed stenosis has the same diameter in inspiration and expiration.
It caps peak flow in both directions, so both limbs of the loop flatten into plateaus.
Her own restrictive disease gives a narrow loop at low lung volumes, which looks different.
questions.why: Flow-volume loops show where airflow is limited. A fixed upper airway obstruction, such as tracheal stenosis after prolonged intubation, flattens both the inspiratory and expiratory limbs. A variable extrathoracic obstruction, such as vocal cord paralysis, flattens only the inspiratory limb, because negative airway pressure pulls the lesion inward during inspiration. Obstructive disease gives a scooped expiratory limb with a low FEV1/FVC ratio and normal or increased total lung capacity. Restrictive disease gives a narrow loop at low lung volumes with a normal or increased FEV1/FVC ratio.
whyNot: A scooped expiratory limb with a high total lung capacity is the pattern of obstructive disease such as COPD.
Correct.
A narrow loop shifted toward low volumes is the restrictive pattern of her interstitial lung disease.
Flattening of only the inspiratory limb fits a variable extrathoracic obstruction, such as vocal cord paralysis.

questions.stem: Her inflammation is centered on the bronchioles. Compared with the epithelium lining a bronchus, the epithelium lining a normal terminal bronchiole shows which of the following changes?
options: Cilia are absent and goblet cells are more numerous
Basal cells give way to type II pneumocytes
Pseudostratified lining becomes stratified squamous
Goblet cells disappear and club cells appear
approach: Bronchi are lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells, resting on a wall with cartilage and submucosal glands.
Moving distally, the epithelium becomes simple columnar and then simple cuboidal, and goblet cells disappear.
Terminal bronchioles are lined by ciliated cuboidal cells and club cells.
questions.why: The airway lining thins step by step. The trachea and bronchi have pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells. Bronchioles lose cartilage and glands, and in terminal bronchioles the lining is simple cuboidal with ciliated cells and club cells. Club cells secrete protective proteins, metabolize inhaled toxins with cytochrome P450 enzymes, and act as progenitor cells for the bronchiolar lining. Respiratory bronchioles have alveoli opening from their walls, and the alveoli themselves are lined by type I and type II pneumocytes.
whyNot: Cilia persist down to the terminal bronchioles, and goblet cells become fewer, not more numerous, as airways narrow.
Type II pneumocytes line the alveoli, not the terminal bronchioles.
The bronchial tree does not normally become stratified squamous. That change is squamous metaplasia, seen with smoking or vitamin A deficiency.
Correct.

topics: Airway epithelium from trachea to alveoli

dx: Anti-glomerular basement membrane (Goodpasture) syndrome with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage and glomerulonephritis
case: A 24-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of coughing up blood for 2 days. He has had fatigue and dark urine for 2 weeks. He smokes 1 pack of cigarettes daily. His temperature is 37.2 °C (99.0 °F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 154/96 mm Hg. Oxygen saturation is 91% on room air. Crackles are heard over both lungs. Hemoglobin concentration is 9.4 g/dL (13.5 to 17.5), and serum creatinine concentration is 3.6 mg/dL (0.7 to 1.3). Urinalysis shows red blood cell casts. A chest x-ray shows bilateral patchy alveolar opacities. Serum anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies are present, and ANCA testing is negative. The diagnosis is anti-glomerular basement membrane (Goodpasture) syndrome with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage and glomerulonephritis.

questions.stem: A kidney biopsy shows crescents in most glomeruli. Which of the following immunofluorescence findings and mechanisms of injury are most likely?
options: Granular IgG and C3; type III hypersensitivity
Scant immune deposits; ANCA-mediated vasculitis
Linear IgG and C3; type II hypersensitivity
Mesangial IgA deposits; type III hypersensitivity
approach: Anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies are IgG directed at a fixed tissue antigen, the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen.
Antibody binding directly to a tissue antigen is type II hypersensitivity.
Because the antigen is spread evenly along the basement membrane, immunofluorescence shows smooth linear IgG, often with C3.
questions.why: In Goodpasture syndrome, IgG binds the noncollagenous domain of the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen in glomerular and alveolar basement membranes. Complement and neutrophils then injure the membrane, causing crescentic glomerulonephritis and alveolar hemorrhage. Smoking and other lung injury expose the alveolar antigen and make hemorrhage more likely. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis can look similar but is a pauci-immune necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis of the upper and lower airways and kidneys, usually with PR3-ANCA. Immune complex diseases such as lupus nephritis give granular deposits instead.
whyNot: Granular deposits of IgG and C3 come from immune complexes (type III), as in lupus nephritis or poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.
Scant deposits with ANCA describe pauci-immune vasculitis such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis. His ANCA test is negative.
Correct.
Mesangial IgA deposits define IgA nephropathy, which causes hematuria but not anti-basement membrane antibodies or lung hemorrhage.

questions.stem: His diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO) is measured on the day of admission. Which of the following best predicts the result?
options: Increased, because red cells in alveoli bind CO
Decreased, because blood thickens the barrier
Decreased, because anemia lowers capillary hemoglobin
Unchanged, because CO uptake is perfusion limited
approach: CO uptake is diffusion limited: hemoglobin binds CO so avidly that plasma CO partial pressure stays near zero.
Measured CO uptake therefore depends on how much hemoglobin the gas can reach.
Red cells that have bled into the alveoli also take up CO, so the measured DLCO rises despite his anemia.
questions.why: By Fick law, diffusion is proportional to surface area and the partial pressure difference and inversely proportional to barrier thickness. Gases differ in what limits their transfer. N2O, and O2 at rest, equilibrate early in the capillary, so their uptake is perfusion limited. CO never equilibrates, so its uptake is diffusion limited, which is why it is used to test the membrane. DLCO falls in emphysema (less surface area) and pulmonary fibrosis (thicker barrier). In acute alveolar hemorrhage, blood in the airspaces raises DLCO, and a new rise can signal fresh bleeding.
whyNot: Correct.
Blood in the alveoli acts as extra hemoglobin for CO to bind, which outweighs any barrier effect.
Anemia does lower DLCO, but alveolar blood raises the measured value more in acute hemorrhage.
CO uptake is diffusion limited, not perfusion limited. N2O is the classic perfusion-limited gas.

questions.stem: The antibodies in this disorder bind an antigen within the blood-air barrier, but they reach it mainly after the capillary endothelium has been injured, for example by cigarette smoke. Which component of the barrier contains this antigen?
options: Surfactant film lining the alveolar surface
Apical membrane of type I pneumocytes
Cytoplasm of capillary endothelial cells
Fused basement membrane
approach: The target antigen is type IV collagen, a basement membrane protein.
In the thin part of the blood-air barrier, the type I pneumocyte and capillary endothelium share one fused basement membrane.
Antibodies in the blood must cross the endothelium to reach it, which is easier after endothelial injury.
questions.why: The blood-air barrier has three layers: type I pneumocyte, fused basement membranes, and capillary endothelium. Its thinness allows rapid gas diffusion. In the glomerulus, the endothelium is fenestrated, so circulating antibodies reach the basement membrane easily, which is why kidney disease is nearly universal in this syndrome. Lung capillaries have continuous endothelium, so alveolar hemorrhage occurs mainly when smoking, infection, or other injury makes the endothelium leaky. Any process that thickens the barrier, such as edema or fibrosis, slows diffusion.
whyNot: The surfactant film lines the air side of the alveolus and contains lipids and proteins, not type IV collagen.
Type I pneumocytes form the epithelial layer. Their apical membrane faces the air and does not hold the target antigen.
Endothelial cytoplasm is a layer the antibodies must cross. It does not contain type IV collagen.
Correct.

questions.stem: Two weeks later, after plasmapheresis and immunosuppressive treatment, his lungs have cleared, but his hemoglobin concentration is 7.6 g/dL. Which of the following sets of arterial values is most likely?
options: Low PaO2, low SaO2, low O2 content
Normal PaO2, normal SaO2, low O2 content
Normal PaO2, low SaO2, low O2 content
Normal PaO2, normal SaO2, normal O2 content
approach: With healthy lungs, PaO2 is normal, and SaO2 depends on PaO2, so it is also normal.
O2 content is about 1.34 x hemoglobin x SaO2, plus a small dissolved amount (0.003 x PaO2).
With hemoglobin of 7.6 g/dL, content is about 10 mL O2/dL, half of normal. This is anemic hypoxia.
questions.why: Hypoxemia means a low PaO2. Hypoxia means too little O2 reaching tissues, and it has four main types. Hypoxemic hypoxia (lung disease, high altitude, hypoventilation) lowers PaO2, SaO2, and content. Anemic hypoxia keeps PaO2 and SaO2 normal but lowers content. Circulatory hypoxia, as in shock, leaves arterial values normal but delivers too little blood. Histotoxic hypoxia, as in cyanide poisoning, leaves arterial values normal, but cells cannot use O2, so venous O2 stays high. Carbon monoxide gives a normal PaO2 with low true saturation and content.
whyNot: Low PaO2 and SaO2 indicate hypoxemic hypoxia from a lung problem. His lungs have cleared.
Correct.
A normal PaO2 with low SaO2 is the pattern of carbon monoxide poisoning or methemoglobinemia, where hemoglobin cannot bind O2 normally.
Normal content would require normal hemoglobin. His hemoglobin is about half of normal.

dx: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis in a young adult with cystic fibrosis
case: A 21-year-old man with cystic fibrosis comes to the physician because of 3 weeks of increased cough, wheezing, and brown mucus plugs in his sputum. He is homozygous for the F508del CFTR variant. His temperature is 37.4 °C (99.3 °F). Expiratory wheezes and coarse crackles are heard over both lungs. Leukocyte count is 9,800/mm3 with 14% eosinophils (normal 1 to 6), and total serum IgE concentration is 2,400 IU/mL (normal below 100). Aspergillus-specific IgE and IgG are increased. Chest CT shows central bronchiectasis with mucus plugging and new patchy infiltrates. The diagnosis is allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis in a young adult with cystic fibrosis.

questions.stem: His parents are healthy, and his older sister does not have cystic fibrosis. Which of the following is the probability that his sister is a carrier of a disease-causing CFTR variant?
approach: Cystic fibrosis is autosomal recessive, so his healthy parents must both be carriers.
A child of two carriers has a 1/4 chance of being unaffected noncarrier, 1/2 carrier, and 1/4 affected.
The sister is known to be unaffected, so only the three unaffected outcomes remain. Two of those three are carriers, giving 2/3.
questions.why: CFTR is on chromosome 7 and encodes an ATP-gated chloride channel. The most common variant, F508del, causes the protein to misfold, so it is held in the endoplasmic reticulum and degraded by the proteasome instead of reaching the cell surface. Less chloride is secreted, and airway mucus becomes thick and dehydrated. In carrier risk problems, always remove outcomes that the facts rule out. Knowing the sister is unaffected changes her carrier risk from 1/2 to 2/3.
whyNot: 1/4 is the chance that any child of two carriers is affected, not the carrier risk of an unaffected sibling.
1/2 is the carrier risk before we know whether the child is affected. It ignores the fact that the sister is unaffected.
Correct.
3/4 is the chance that a child of two carriers is unaffected, not the chance that an unaffected child is a carrier.

topics: Autosomal recessive inheritance and carrier risk

questions.stem: His sweat chloride concentration, measured in childhood, was 104 mmol/L (normal below 30). Which of the following best explains this result?
options: Excess chloride secretion by the secretory coil
Failed chloride reabsorption in the sweat duct
Excess sodium absorption through ENaC in the duct
Aldosterone resistance in sweat duct cells
approach: The sweat gland coil secretes a fluid similar in salt content to plasma.
As sweat passes up the duct, CFTR reabsorbs chloride, and ENaC reabsorbs sodium, so normal sweat reaching the skin is hypotonic.
Without working CFTR, chloride stays in the duct, and sodium absorption also falls, so the sweat stays salty.
questions.why: CFTR moves chloride in different directions in different tissues. In the sweat duct, the epithelium is absorptive, and CFTR takes chloride back out of the sweat. Loss of CFTR leaves high chloride in sweat, and a sweat chloride of 60 mmol/L or higher supports the diagnosis. In the airway, CFTR normally secretes chloride into the airway surface liquid and restrains ENaC. In cystic fibrosis, chloride secretion falls, sodium absorption through ENaC increases, and water follows the sodium out of the airway, leaving thick, dehydrated mucus.
whyNot: Primary sweat secretion in the coil is near normal in cystic fibrosis. The defect is in reabsorption along the duct.
Correct.
In the sweat duct, sodium absorption falls along with chloride absorption. Excess ENaC sodium absorption happens in the airway epithelium.
Aldosterone resistance (pseudohypoaldosteronism) can raise sweat salt, but this patient has a CFTR defect, not a hormone receptor defect.

topics: CFTR in sweat duct and airway

questions.stem: Microscopy of his sputum mucus plugs shows narrow septate hyphae with acute-angle branching. In which of the following patients would this same organism most likely invade lung tissue and blood vessels?
options: Man with HIV infection and a CD4 count of 150/mm3
Woman with selective IgA deficiency and sinusitis
Man with terminal complement (C5 to C9) deficiency
Woman with severe neutropenia from chemotherapy
approach: Narrow septate hyphae branching at acute angles identify Aspergillus.
Neutrophils are the main defense against Aspergillus hyphae, and macrophages kill inhaled conidia.
Prolonged severe neutropenia lets hyphae grow through tissue and invade vessels, causing hemorrhagic infarcts.
questions.why: Aspergillus fumigatus is a mold found in soil and decaying vegetation. How it affects the lung depends on the host. In airways damaged by asthma or cystic fibrosis, it can colonize mucus and provoke allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. In an old cavity it can form an aspergilloma. With prolonged neutropenia, high-dose corticosteroids, or transplant immunosuppression, it causes invasive angioinvasive aspergillosis. By contrast, Pneumocystis jirovecii causes pneumonia when the CD4 count falls below 200 cells/mm3 and is seen as cysts on methenamine silver stain.
whyNot: A CD4 count below 200 cells/mm3 is the classic risk for Pneumocystis pneumonia. Invasive aspergillosis in HIV is uncommon until counts are far lower.
Selective IgA deficiency leads to recurrent sinopulmonary bacterial infections and Giardia, not invasive mold infection.
Terminal complement deficiency predisposes to recurrent Neisseria infections.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the process causing his current lung disease?
options: Hypersensitivity to fungi colonizing airway mucus
Fungal invasion through the walls of pulmonary vessels
A fungal ball growing inside an old lung cavity
Cysts filling alveoli with foamy eosinophilic exudate
approach: His findings are eosinophilia, very high total IgE, Aspergillus-specific IgE and IgG, mucus plugs, and central bronchiectasis.
These point to an allergic reaction to Aspergillus growing in airway mucus, not tissue invasion.
This is allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, which develops in people with asthma or cystic fibrosis.
questions.why: Aspergillus causes several distinct lung diseases. Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis is a type I and type III hypersensitivity to fungus colonizing thick airway mucus, with eosinophilia, very high IgE, brown mucus plugs, and central bronchiectasis. Aspergilloma is a fungus ball in an old cavity, such as one left by tuberculosis, and often presents with hemoptysis. Invasive aspergillosis occurs in neutropenic or heavily immunosuppressed patients and causes nodules with surrounding hemorrhage. Pneumocystis pneumonia occurs with CD4 counts below 200 cells/mm3 and causes bilateral ground-glass infiltrates, hypoxemia with exertion, and a high LDH.
whyNot: Correct.
Vessel invasion is invasive aspergillosis, seen with severe neutropenia. He is not immunosuppressed and has no infarcts.
A fungus ball in an old cavity is an aspergilloma. His CT shows bronchiectasis and mucus plugs, not a cavity with a mass.
Cysts in a foamy alveolar exudate describe Pneumocystis pneumonia in a patient with a low CD4 count.

dx: Heritable pulmonary arterial hypertension (BMPR2 mutation) with right-to-left shunting through a patent foramen ovale
case: A 31-year-old woman comes to the physician because of exertional shortness of breath that has worsened over 1 year and two episodes of syncope while climbing stairs. Her mother died of pulmonary hypertension at age 40. Pulse is 96/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 108/70 mm Hg. Oxygen saturation is 89% on room air. There is a loud pulmonic component of the second heart sound and a right ventricular heave. Right heart catheterization shows a mean pulmonary arterial pressure of 58 mm Hg (normal 20 or less) and a pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 8 mm Hg (normal 6 to 12). Echocardiography with agitated saline shows right-to-left shunting through a patent foramen ovale. Genetic testing shows a BMPR2 mutation. The diagnosis is heritable pulmonary arterial hypertension with right-to-left shunting through a patent foramen ovale.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes how her mutation leads to this disease?
options: Gain of function in endothelin receptors on smooth muscle
Defective fibrillin weakening the arterial media
Loss of endoglin in pulmonary endothelial cells
Loss of signals that restrain arterial cell growth
approach: BMPR2 encodes a receptor in the TGF-beta superfamily.
Its signaling normally restrains proliferation and favors apoptosis of pulmonary arterial smooth muscle and endothelial cells.
Loss of one working copy lets these cells proliferate, narrowing small pulmonary arteries and raising resistance.
questions.why: Pulmonary hypertension is grouped by cause: pulmonary arterial hypertension (idiopathic, heritable such as BMPR2, drugs, connective tissue disease), left heart disease, lung disease or hypoxia, chronic thromboembolism, and other causes. Her normal wedge pressure rules out left heart disease. In pulmonary arterial hypertension, the small arteries show medial hypertrophy, intimal fibrosis, and plexiform lesions, which are tufts of small vascular channels. Endothelial dysfunction lowers nitric oxide and prostacyclin and raises endothelin. Only a minority of BMPR2 carriers develop disease, so other triggers are needed. The right ventricle hypertrophies and eventually fails (cor pulmonale). Her high right atrial pressure pushes blood from right to left through her patent foramen ovale.
whyNot: Endothelin levels rise in pulmonary arterial hypertension, which is why endothelin blockers are used, but BMPR2 mutation is not a gain of function in endothelin receptors.
Defective fibrillin causes Marfan syndrome, which weakens the aortic media and leads to aneurysm and dissection.
Loss of endoglin causes hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia with arteriovenous malformations.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her pulmonary arterial pressure falls slightly when she breathes supplemental oxygen. Which of the following correctly compares how pulmonary and systemic arterioles respond to hypoxia?
options: Pulmonary constrict; systemic dilate
Pulmonary dilate; systemic constrict
Pulmonary and systemic both constrict
Pulmonary and systemic both dilate
approach: Low alveolar PO2 causes pulmonary arterioles to constrict (hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction).
This sends blood away from poorly ventilated alveoli and improves ventilation-perfusion matching.
Systemic arterioles dilate in hypoxia, which increases blood flow to tissues that need more O2.
questions.why: In pulmonary arteriolar smooth muscle, hypoxia inhibits O2-sensitive potassium channels. The cells depolarize, calcium enters, and the vessels constrict. In systemic beds, hypoxia causes dilation through local metabolites such as adenosine, nitric oxide, and opening of ATP-sensitive potassium channels. Chronic alveolar hypoxia, as in COPD or high altitude, causes sustained pulmonary vasoconstriction, vascular remodeling, pulmonary hypertension, and right ventricular hypertrophy (cor pulmonale). In her disease, the main cause is the arterial remodeling, but hypoxemia adds a small reversible component, which is why oxygen lowers her pressure slightly.
whyNot: Correct.
This is the reverse of the true responses.
Systemic arterioles dilate in hypoxia to match flow to tissue need.
Pulmonary arterioles constrict in hypoxia. Dilation would send blood to poorly ventilated alveoli and worsen oxygenation.

questions.stem: In a healthy adult, the pulmonary circulation carries the entire cardiac output at a mean arterial pressure of about 15 mm Hg. Which of the following features best explains this low pressure?
options: Smaller right ventricular stroke volume
Thin, distensible arteries with little smooth muscle
Constant sympathetic dilation of pulmonary arteries
Nutrient supply of lung tissue by bronchial arteries
approach: Pressure depends on flow and resistance, and both ventricles pump the same flow.
Pulmonary arteries have thin walls with little smooth muscle and are very distensible, so resistance is low, roughly one tenth of systemic resistance.
When cardiac output rises, unopened capillaries are recruited and open vessels distend, so resistance falls further and pressure barely rises.
questions.why: The pulmonary circulation is a low-pressure, low-resistance system. Its main job is gas exchange. The bronchial arteries are a separate systemic supply, arising from the aorta at systemic pressure, that nourishes the airways, pleura, and supporting tissue. Some bronchial venous blood drains into the pulmonary veins, adding a small normal shunt. Because the lung has this dual supply, pulmonary emboli usually do not cause infarction unless bronchial flow is also poor. In pulmonary arterial hypertension, remodeled thick-walled arteries lose this low resistance.
whyNot: Right and left ventricular stroke volumes are equal over time. The pressures differ because resistance differs.
Correct.
Sympathetic nerves have little effect on pulmonary vessel tone, and the pulmonary vessels are not held open by them.
Bronchial arteries do supply lung tissue, but they are a separate systemic circuit. They do not explain pressure in the pulmonary arteries.

questions.stem: Which of the following arterial blood gas patterns is most likely to result from her right-to-left shunt?
options: Low PaO2 and high PaCO2 from hypoventilation
Normal PaO2 and high PaCO2 from dead space
Low PaO2 and normal or low PaCO2
Normal PaO2 and low PaCO2 from anxiety
approach: A shunt (V/Q of zero) sends venous blood into the arterial circulation without passing ventilated alveoli, so PaO2 falls.
The CO2 added by shunted blood raises PaCO2 only slightly, and the chemoreceptors respond by increasing ventilation.
Because the CO2 curve is nearly linear, extra ventilation easily clears CO2, so PaCO2 stays normal or low while PaO2 remains low.
questions.why: Shunt and dead space are the two ends of ventilation-perfusion mismatch. In a shunt, blood passes without meeting air, as with an intracardiac right-to-left shunt or alveoli filled by pneumonia or edema. PaO2 falls, and extra O2 helps little, because the ventilated units already carry nearly saturated hemoglobin and cannot make up for the shunted blood. In dead space (V/Q approaching infinity), as in pulmonary embolism, ventilation reaches alveoli without blood flow. It wastes ventilation and tends to raise PaCO2 unless total ventilation increases.
whyNot: Hypoventilation raises PaCO2 and lowers PaO2 with a normal A-a gradient. Her drive to breathe is intact.
Dead space wastes ventilation and can raise PaCO2, but it does not describe her shunt, which lowers PaO2.
Correct.
Anxiety can lower PaCO2, but a shunt this large lowers PaO2, as her low oxygen saturation shows.

dx: Acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema from left ventricular failure after myocardial infarction
case: A 66-year-old man develops severe shortness of breath 2 days after admission to the hospital for an anterior wall myocardial infarction. He coughs up frothy pink sputum. His temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 122/min, respirations are 32/min, and blood pressure is 88/56 mm Hg. Oxygen saturation is 84% on room air. Crackles are heard over both lungs, loudest at the bases, and an S3 gallop is present. Serum lactate concentration is 5.8 mmol/L (0.5 to 2.2). A chest x-ray shows bilateral perihilar opacities and Kerley B lines. Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is 28 mm Hg (normal 6 to 12), and echocardiography shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 25%. The diagnosis is acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema from left ventricular failure after myocardial infarction.

questions.stem: Which of the following changes in Starling forces most directly explains the fluid in his alveoli?
options: Increased capillary permeability to protein
Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure
Decreased plasma colloid osmotic pressure
Decreased lymphatic drainage of the interstitium
approach: His failing left ventricle cannot empty, so left atrial pressure rises, shown by a wedge pressure of 28 mm Hg.
That pressure is transmitted back to the pulmonary veins and capillaries.
Higher capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid into the interstitium faster than lymphatics can remove it, and the fluid then floods the alveoli.
questions.why: Starling forces set fluid movement across capillaries: hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out, and plasma oncotic pressure pulls it back. Lung lymphatics can increase their flow several times over, which protects the lung until wedge pressure exceeds about 18 to 25 mm Hg. Cardiogenic edema fluid is low in protein. Chronic congestion causes small hemorrhages, and alveolar macrophages that eat the red cells become hemosiderin-laden heart failure cells. Noncardiogenic edema comes from capillary injury (ARDS), low oncotic pressure (nephrotic syndrome, liver failure), or blocked lymphatics, and it occurs with a normal wedge pressure.
whyNot: Increased permeability causes noncardiogenic edema, as in ARDS, with a normal wedge pressure. His wedge pressure is high.
Correct.
Low plasma oncotic pressure occurs with nephrotic syndrome or liver failure. It does not explain sudden edema after a myocardial infarction.
Lymphatic obstruction, as in lymphangitic tumor spread, causes slowly progressive edema. His lymphatics are working hard but are overwhelmed.

questions.stem: His crackles are loudest at the lung bases, where edema forms first in an upright person. Which of the following orders of alveolar, pulmonary arterial, and pulmonary venous pressure describes the lung bases in an upright person?
options: Alveolar > arterial > venous
Arterial > alveolar > venous
Venous > arterial > alveolar
Arterial > venous > alveolar
approach: Gravity raises vascular pressures toward the bottom of the upright lung, while alveolar pressure is about the same everywhere.
At the bases, both arterial and venous pressures exceed alveolar pressure. This is zone 3.
Flow is continuous and capillary hydrostatic pressure is highest in zone 3, so edema appears there first.
questions.why: West zones describe how the balance of alveolar, arterial, and venous pressures changes from apex to base. Zone 1 (alveolar > arterial > venous) has no flow and is normally absent. It appears with hemorrhage or high positive-pressure ventilation. Zone 2 (arterial > alveolar > venous), toward the apex, has flow that depends on the arterial-alveolar difference. Zone 3 (arterial > venous > alveolar), at the bases, has continuous flow. Both ventilation and perfusion are greater at the base, but perfusion rises more, so the ventilation-perfusion ratio is highest at the apex and lowest at the base.
whyNot: Alveolar pressure above arterial pressure is zone 1, where capillaries collapse. It is not present at the bases.
Arterial above alveolar above venous is zone 2, found in the middle to upper lung.
Venous pressure cannot exceed arterial pressure in normal forward flow.
Correct.

questions.stem: His lactate is high because his tissues are poorly perfused. When oxygen is not available to accept electrons, which of the following is the net ATP yield per molecule of glucose in his tissues?
approach: O2 is the final electron acceptor at cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV). Without it, the electron transport chain stops, and oxidative phosphorylation stops.
NADH cannot be reoxidized by mitochondria, so the citric acid cycle also slows to a halt.
Only glycolysis continues, which nets 2 ATP per glucose when pyruvate is reduced to lactate.
questions.why: Complete oxidation of glucose with O2 yields about 30 to 32 ATP. In anaerobic conditions, glycolysis makes 4 ATP but uses 2, for a net of 2. To keep glycolysis running, lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate to lactate and regenerates NAD+. Because so little ATP is made this way, cells consume glucose rapidly and lactate builds up, causing type A lactic acidosis. In cardiogenic shock, low cardiac output reduces O2 delivery to tissues and produces exactly this pattern.
whyNot: Correct.
4 ATP is the gross yield of glycolysis. Two ATP are spent in the early steps, so the net yield is 2.
About 7 ATP would come from glycolysis plus reoxidation of its NADH in mitochondria. That needs O2.
About 30 to 32 ATP is the yield of complete aerobic oxidation of glucose, which needs O2 at complex IV.

questions.stem: His high central venous pressure also slows the return of lymph from the thoracic duct into the venous system. At which of the following sites does the thoracic duct normally drain?
options: Right subclavian and right internal jugular junction
Azygos vein at the level of the fourth thoracic vertebra
Left subclavian and left internal jugular junction
Superior vena cava at its entry into the right atrium
approach: The thoracic duct begins at the cisterna chyli in the abdomen and enters the thorax through the aortic hiatus.
It ascends behind the esophagus, crosses to the left at about T4 to T6, and rises into the root of the neck.
It empties at the junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins, so lymph flow depends on venous pressure there.
questions.why: The thoracic duct drains lymph from the whole body below the diaphragm and from the left side of the thorax, head, neck, and left arm. The right lymphatic duct drains the right upper body and empties at the right venous angle. Lymph moves into the veins only when lymphatic pressure exceeds venous pressure, so a high central venous pressure slows lymph return and adds to edema and effusions in heart failure. Injury to the duct from trauma, surgery, or tumor causes chylothorax, with milky, triglyceride-rich pleural fluid.
whyNot: The right venous angle receives the right lymphatic duct, not the thoracic duct.
The thoracic duct runs near the azygos vein in the posterior mediastinum but does not drain into it.
Correct.
The thoracic duct does not enter the superior vena cava. It ends at the left venous angle in the root of the neck.
